questions.stem: Which statement describes the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom?
options: The electron is spread evenly through a positively charged sphere, like fruit in a pudding
The electron can have any energy and spirals slowly into the nucleus as it radiates
The electron sits inside the nucleus and is released when the atom absorbs energy
The electron moves in fixed orbits of set energy, changing energy only by jumping
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed that the electron can occupy only certain orbits, each with a fixed energy, and that it absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps from one level to another. The evenly spread positive sphere is the earlier Thomson model.

questions.stem: Why does hydrogen gas in a discharge tube emit light of only certain wavelengths?
options: Hydrogen molecules vibrate at certain frequencies, emitting heat of those frequencies
The nucleus releases particles of set energy as it becomes unstable
The glass of the tube absorbs every other wavelength of the light
Electrons fall between fixed energy levels, emitting photons of particular energies
questions.explanation: Excited electrons drop from higher to lower energy levels, and each drop releases a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels. Since only certain gaps exist, only certain wavelengths appear, giving a line spectrum.

questions.stem: White light passes through cool sodium vapour. Dark lines appear in the spectrum at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in sodium's emission spectrum. Why?
options: The vapour reflects light of those wavelengths back towards the light source
Cool sodium vapour absorbs every wavelength except those of its emission lines
Sodium electrons absorb photons that match the gaps between energy levels
Sodium atoms emit light at those wavelengths, which cancels out the white light
questions.explanation: An electron can only absorb a photon whose energy exactly matches a jump to a higher level. Those are the same energy gaps that produce the emission lines when electrons fall back, so the dark absorption lines line up with the bright emission lines.

questions.stem: Why can the line spectrum of an element be used to identify it, even in a distant star?
options: Each element has its own energy levels, so its pattern of lines is unique
Each element emits light of a single colour that no other element produces
The brightness of the lines depends only on the element's atomic mass number
Every element produces a continuous spectrum of a characteristic width
questions.explanation: The spacing of energy levels depends on the number of protons and electrons, so every element has a unique set of energy gaps and therefore a unique pattern of lines. Most elements give several lines, not a single colour.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen atom, which electron transition emits the photon with the highest energy?
options: From n = 4 to n = 3
From n = 1 to n = 3
From n = 3 to n = 1
From n = 2 to n = 1
questions.explanation: Energy levels get closer together as n increases, so the biggest gap here is between n = 3 and n = 1. A jump from n = 1 to n = 3 is upwards, which absorbs a photon rather than emitting one.

questions.stem: What does the principal quantum number, n, of an electron indicate?
options: The shape of the orbital that the electron occupies
The direction in which the electron is spinning
The shell, or main energy level, that the electron occupies
The number of electrons in the electron's shell
questions.explanation: The principal quantum number labels the shell: n = 1 is the lowest energy level, closest to the nucleus. The shape of an orbital (s, p or d) is described by a different quantum number, and spin by another.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that a single orbital can hold?
questions.explanation: Any orbital, whether s, p or d, holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. Six is the capacity of a p sub-shell (three orbitals), and eight is a full s plus p set.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons the n = 3 shell can hold?
questions.explanation: The third shell has 3s (1 orbital), 3p (3 orbitals) and 3d (5 orbitals), so 9 orbitals × 2 = 18 electrons, matching 2n². Eight is the number in a full outer shell of argon, where 3d is empty.

questions.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of a sulfur atom (Z = 16)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁴ 3s² 3p⁶
questions.explanation: Sixteen electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p and 3s (12 electrons) and leave 4 in 3p. 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ has 18 electrons, which is the sulfide ion or argon, and the others skip or underfill a lower sub-shell.

questions.stem: In a potassium atom, the 19th electron enters the 4s sub-shell rather than the 3d sub-shell. Why?
options: The 4s sub-shell is lower in energy than the 3d sub-shell
The 3d sub-shell can only fill once the whole n = 4 shell is full
The 4s sub-shell is closer to the nucleus than the 3d sub-shell
The 3d sub-shell can hold only two electrons, and they are paired
questions.explanation: Electrons fill the lowest-energy sub-shell available, and 4s is slightly lower in energy than 3d. So potassium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹, and 3d starts to fill only after 4s, at scandium. A d sub-shell holds ten electrons.

questions.stem: How many electrons are in the 3d sub-shell of a ground-state iron atom (Z = 26)?
questions.explanation: Argon's configuration accounts for 18 electrons, 4s takes 2 more, and the remaining 26 − 20 = 6 go into 3d. Answering 8 forgets that 4s fills before 3d.

questions.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the chloride ion, Cl⁻?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
questions.explanation: A chlorine atom has 17 electrons (3p⁵); gaining one electron fills the 3p sub-shell, giving 18 electrons. 3p⁵ is the neutral atom, and adding a 4s electron would give 19.

questions.stem: An atom has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. Where is it in the periodic table?
options: Group 15, period 3
Group 3, period 3
Group 13, period 3
Group 15, period 5
questions.explanation: The highest shell is n = 3, so it is in period 3, and its five outer electrons (3s² 3p³) place it in group 15: it is phosphorus. Group 13 would end in 3p¹.

questions.stem: Na⁺, F⁻ and Ne are described as isoelectronic. What does this mean?
options: They have the same overall charge and the same ionic radius
They have the same number of electrons, in the same configuration
They have the same number of protons in their nuclei
They have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell only
questions.explanation: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons: each of these has 10, as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. They differ in their number of protons, which is why their charges and radii differ.

questions.stem: Which of these species is isoelectronic with argon?
options: Na⁺
Ca²⁺
Mg²⁺
Br⁻
questions.explanation: Calcium has 20 electrons, and losing two leaves 18, the same as argon. Mg²⁺ and Na⁺ have 10 electrons, like neon, and Br⁻ has 36, like krypton.

questions.stem: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ are isoelectronic. Which has the largest radius?
options: F⁻
O²⁻
Mg²⁺
Na⁺
questions.explanation: All four have 10 electrons in the same arrangement, but O²⁻ has only 8 protons pulling on them, the fewest of the four, so its electron cloud is held least tightly and is largest. Mg²⁺, with 12 protons, is the smallest.

questions.stem: Selenium is in group 16. What is the charge on its most common simple ion?
questions.explanation: With six outer electrons, selenium most easily gains two to reach a stable noble gas configuration, forming Se²⁻ like oxygen and sulfur. Losing six electrons would take far more energy.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energy of potassium is 419 kJ mol⁻¹. What process does this value refer to?
options: Removing one electron from each atom in a mole of gaseous potassium atoms
Adding one electron to each atom in a mole of gaseous potassium atoms
Removing every electron from each atom in a mole of gaseous potassium
Breaking the metallic bonding in a mole of solid potassium metal
questions.explanation: First ionisation energy is the energy for K(g) → K⁺(g) + e⁻, per mole of atoms. Adding an electron is a different process, removing further electrons involves the second and later ionisation energies, and breaking metallic bonding is atomisation of the solid.

questions.stem: Why is each successive ionisation energy of an atom larger than the one before?
options: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion
Each electron removed adds a proton to the nucleus of the remaining ion
The remaining electrons move into higher shells, further from the nucleus
The atom gains neutrons as it loses electrons, increasing its mass
questions.explanation: After each removal, the same number of protons pulls on fewer electrons, and there is less repulsion between them, so the next electron is harder to remove. The nucleus does not change during ionisation.

questions.stem: An element's first five ionisation energies, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 738, 1451, 7733, 10 543 and 13 630. Which group is it in?
options: Group 5
Group 1
Group 2
Group 3
questions.explanation: The big jump comes between the second and third ionisation energies, so the first two electrons are in the outer shell and the third comes from an inner shell. Two outer electrons means group 2: this is magnesium.

questions.stem: A period 3 element has successive ionisation energies of 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. Which element is it?
options: Magnesium
Silicon
Phosphorus
Aluminium
questions.explanation: The large jump is after the third electron, so there are three electrons in the outer shell: group 13. In period 3 that is aluminium. Magnesium would show its jump after the second electron, and silicon after the fourth.

questions.stem: Sodium's second ionisation energy is about nine times its first. Why?
options: The second electron comes from the inner n = 2 shell, which is less shielded
The second electron is removed from the same shell, which is now more crowded
Sodium's nucleus gains a proton after the first electron is removed
The second electron must first be promoted to a higher shell
questions.explanation: Sodium is 2,8,1. Its first electron is a lone 3s electron shielded by ten inner electrons. The second comes from the full n = 2 shell, which is much closer to the nucleus and shielded only by the two 1s electrons, so far more energy is needed.

questions.stem: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across period 3 from sodium to argon?
options: Nuclear charge falls across the period as electrons are added
Core charge increases while the outer electrons remain in the same shell
Each element has one more inner shell to shield its outer electrons
Atomic radius increases, so outer electrons are more spread out
questions.explanation: Across a period protons are added but the inner shells are unchanged, so core charge rises from +1 to +8 and the outer electrons, all in n = 3, are held more tightly. Atomic radius actually decreases across the period.

questions.stem: Aluminium has a lower first ionisation energy than magnesium, against the general trend across period 3. Why?
options: Aluminium has a smaller nuclear charge than magnesium, so attracts electrons less
Aluminium's outer electrons are in the fourth shell, further from the nucleus
Aluminium's outer electron is paired, so repulsion makes it easier to remove
Aluminium's outermost electron is in 3p, higher in energy than 3s
questions.explanation: Magnesium's outer electrons are in 3s, but aluminium's third outer electron is in 3p, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily. Aluminium has more protons than magnesium, not fewer.

questions.stem: What is the core charge of a chlorine atom (2,8,7)?
questions.explanation: Core charge = protons − inner-shell electrons = 17 − 10 = +7. It is the net charge pulling on the outer electrons. +17 is the full nuclear charge, which ignores shielding by the inner shells.

questions.stem: What is meant by shielding in an atom?
options: Neutrons in the nucleus reducing the repulsion between protons
Outer electrons protecting the nucleus from collisions with other atoms
Electrons in the same orbital cancelling each other's charges
Inner-shell electrons reducing the nucleus's attraction for outer electrons
questions.explanation: Electrons in inner shells lie between the nucleus and the outer electrons and repel them, so the outer electrons feel only the core charge rather than the full nuclear charge.

questions.stem: How does the core charge change going down group 17 from fluorine to iodine?
options: It stays the same, at +7
It increases by 8 in each period
It decreases steadily down the group
It increases in step with the nuclear charge
questions.explanation: Going down the group each atom has more protons, but also a whole extra filled inner shell, so protons minus inner electrons stays at +7. The extra shells put the outer electrons further away, which is what changes down a group.

questions.stem: Oxygen is described as highly electronegative. What property of its atoms does this describe?
options: The number of electrons its atom can share in covalent bonds
The charge on the ion that its atom most commonly forms
How strongly its atoms attract the shared electrons in covalent bonds
The energy needed to remove an electron from its gaseous atom
questions.explanation: Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons towards itself, and differences in electronegativity make bonds polar. The energy to remove an electron is ionisation energy, a related but different quantity.

questions.stem: Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?
options: Nitrogen
Sulfur
Phosphorus
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. Oxygen is to the right of nitrogen in period 2 and above sulfur in group 16, so it is the most electronegative of the four.

questions.stem: Fluorine and chlorine both have a core charge of +7, yet fluorine is more electronegative. Why?
options: Fluorine's outer electrons are in the third shell, which is more stable
Fluorine's outer shell is closer to its nucleus, so it attracts bonding electrons more
Fluorine has more protons than chlorine, giving it a larger nuclear charge
Fluorine has more inner electrons, which push bonding electrons towards it
questions.explanation: With the same core charge, the deciding factor is distance. Fluorine's bonding electrons are in the second shell, much closer to the nucleus than chlorine's third-shell electrons, so they feel a stronger pull. Chlorine actually has more protons and more inner electrons.

questions.stem: Which list arranges lithium, sodium and potassium in order of increasing atomic radius?
options: Li < Na < K
K < Na < Li
Na < Li < K
Li < K < Na
questions.explanation: Going down group 1, each element has one more occupied shell, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus. Lithium (2 shells) is smallest and potassium (4 shells) is largest.

questions.stem: Sodium and chlorine are both in period 3. Why is a chlorine atom smaller than a sodium atom?
options: Chlorine's extra electrons repel each other less than sodium's do
Chlorine's larger mass compresses its electron cloud more tightly
Chlorine's higher core charge pulls the same outer shell closer to the nucleus
Chlorine has fewer occupied shells than sodium, so its electrons are closer
questions.explanation: Both atoms have outer electrons in the third shell, but chlorine's core charge is +7 compared with sodium's +1, so its outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the atom is smaller. Both have three occupied shells.

questions.stem: Which comparison of atomic and ionic radii is correct?
options: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are both larger than their atoms
Na⁺ is smaller than Na, and Cl⁻ is larger than Cl
Na⁺ is larger than Na, and Cl⁻ is smaller than Cl
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are both smaller than their atoms
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its only third-shell electron, so Na⁺ has one fewer shell and is much smaller. Chlorine gains an electron in the same shell; the extra repulsion with no extra protons makes Cl⁻ larger than Cl.

questions.stem: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
options: Its outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily
It has a higher core charge, so it attracts water molecules more strongly
It has more outer-shell electrons available to transfer to water
Its outer electron is closer to the nucleus, so it is more energetic
questions.explanation: Both have a core charge of +1, but potassium's outer electron is in the fourth shell, further from the nucleus, so less energy is needed to remove it. Metals react by losing electrons, so the element that loses its electron most easily reacts fastest.

questions.stem: Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?
options: It has the most electrons of any halogen
Its atoms have the highest core charge of the halogens
Its small atoms attract an extra electron most strongly
Its atoms lose their outer electrons most easily
questions.explanation: Halogens react by gaining an electron. All halogens have a core charge of +7, but fluorine's outer shell is closest to the nucleus, so an incoming electron is attracted most strongly. Going down the group the attraction weakens, so reactivity falls.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water, but magnesium reacts only slowly. Which explanation is correct?
options: Magnesium's outer electrons are in a d sub-shell, which is more stable
Magnesium has a lower nuclear charge, so it attracts water molecules less
Magnesium's higher core charge and smaller radius hold its outer electrons more tightly
Magnesium has more occupied shells, so its outer electrons are better shielded
questions.explanation: Going from sodium to magnesium the core charge rises from +1 to +2 while the outer shell stays the same, so the atom is smaller and its outer electrons are harder to remove. Metals become less reactive from left to right for this reason.

questions.stem: Why is chlorine a more reactive non-metal than sulfur?
options: Chlorine loses its outer electrons more easily than sulfur does
Chlorine has a higher core charge, so it attracts electrons more strongly
Chlorine has fewer protons, so its electrons are less tightly held
Chlorine has one more occupied electron shell than sulfur, so it reacts faster
questions.explanation: Non-metals react by gaining electrons. Chlorine's core charge (+7) is higher than sulfur's (+6) with the outer electrons in the same shell, so it pulls in an extra electron more strongly. Non-metals become more reactive from left to right across a period.
